title: Britain's 'most haunted village' is perfect for a spooky autumn break, with woodland walks and cosy pub lunches
excerpt: We go ghost hunting after dark in Pluckley – an atmospheric autumn escape of ancient woodland, historic pubs and unexplained tales
content:
With its distinctive cottages, winding country lanes and far-reaching views across the Weald of Kent, Pluckley has all the makings of an idyllic autumn escape.

It appeared in the 1989 Guinness Book of Records as Britain’s most haunted village, with around a dozen ghosts said to roam its churchyard, woods and quiet lanes.

But behind the supernatural stories lies a more complicated tale – and not everyone in the village is convinced.

Why is Pluckley known as Britain’s most haunted village?

It’s sunny when I arrive in Pluckley. Residents are bustling around the post office, butcher’s shop and pub. I drive slowly past a yew-shaded churchyard, a tiny Victorian schoolhouse and rows of cottages with neat gardens and the arched windows that make many of the local buildings so distinctive.

It’s a historic, idyllic place, which is probably why the original The Darling Buds of May series was filmed here. But I’ve come in search of something rather less wholesome: ghosts.

I’m on the fence, ghost-wise. I’m a sceptical journalist, but I also write ghostly fiction and love the idea that some things are yet to be explained. With so many reported spirits, surely this is the place to put my nerves – and the village’s reputation – to the test?

When I speak to residents, however, the prevailing mood is bemusement. Guy Washer, chair of the parish council and a long-term resident, says he has never seen anything supernatural.

“To be honest, I feel the whole thing has been done to death,” he says.

“It’s all a load of nonsense,” agrees James Buss, my host at The Dering Arms restaurant and B&B. “I’m logical. If something goes bump in the night, it’s probably a tile just falling off the roof.”

Later, I meet local historian Ed Adams in the churchyard of the 900-year-old St Nicholas Church. He has written a book tracing the real history behind many of Pluckley’s ghost stories.

“Many of them come from a local newsagent and journalist called Frederick Sanders,” he explains. “He’d hear tell, for example, of a watercress seller who had accidentally set herself on fire or a screaming man who died at the brickworks after a collapse of clay. These coalesced into ghost stories. He was the first to refer to Pluckley as ‘the home of ghosts’ in the 1950s.”

But plenty of old villages have their own spooky legends, so how did Pluckley become so closely associated with the supernatural?

“In the 1970s, there was a perception that the village was under threat,” Ed says. “New motorways were being built, the Channel Tunnel rail link was in the planning stages and countryside was earmarked for development.

“At the same time, a group of media-savvy commuters had moved in. They began to push out these stories to bring attention to the village. I don’t think they realised how it would take off.”

Ed shows me some of Pluckley’s supposedly haunted locations. We speculate about which grave might belong to the Red Lady said to roam the churchyard, then explore a field near Ricky Buss’s Lane, where the spirit of a schoolmaster is believed to wander.

I close my eyes and try to sense something, but all around me there is fresh air and birdsong. It feels like the opposite of spooky.

Walk through Pluckley’s ‘Screaming Woods’

From the village, I head to Dering Wood, also known as the Screaming Woods. The ancient woodland is particularly beautiful in autumn, when its paths are surrounded by turning leaves.

Online, you’ll find countless ghost hunters running through the trees and scaring themselves silly. During my visit, however, the only screaming comes from me when I walk through a cobweb and discover a spider clinging to my shoulder.

In daylight, with the leaves turning overhead, the wood feels far more enchanting than eerie. But with its tangle of paths and darker corners, I can see how its ghostly reputation took hold.

Inside one of Pluckley’s haunted pubs

As the sun goes down, I seek solace at the Black Horse, a historic inn that embraces the village’s spooky reputation. Several generations of landlords and landladies are said to have experienced poltergeist-like activity here.

At first, it seems like a normal country pub: exposed beams, a colourful carpet, football on the television and comforting pub food. But there is one difference – almost everyone behind the bar has a ghost story.

Manager James says he has seen candles tumble out of their holders and a hat fly across the room. Chef Darren, who lives upstairs, reports feeling sudden temperature changes as he walks from one room to another.

Landlady Emma Ashby has developed the habit of greeting the pub’s unseen residents whenever she goes upstairs. When she first took over, she brought her team from another pub to complete a deep clean and they stayed overnight.

“At 3am, the wardrobe doors in my room started rattling,” she says. “I went downstairs and found three of my staff looking scared. One of my waitresses had woken at the same time, feeling as if she was being suffocated. It was weird.”

As I eat, a circle of mediums from the surrounding area arrives. When I introduce myself, they are warm and welcoming, so I ask how they believe it all works.

“Spirits are all around us,” says their leader, Sue Roberts. “They’ve passed over, but are not sitting on a cloud somewhere. They’re here, like little specks of light, and they impress themselves on you.”

As the pub grows darker, the group begins to sense activity. Sue speaks with such conviction that I follow them upstairs.

The wonky, sloping rooms are eerie even before we ascend winding, cobwebbed stairs to an attic straight out of a horror film. There are no lights, only our phone torches glinting against the outlines of two scythes that have been stored there for goodness knows how long.

The circle falls silent. I wait, quietly terrified.

They sense a man and a great anger. One suggests a wounded shoulder; another says he is struggling to breathe – an unsettling echo of what Emma’s waitress experienced.

What happens in Pluckley after dark?

Outside the pub, the village has been transformed. There is little street lighting to break up the enveloping darkness, and my earlier plan to explore the churchyard alone suddenly seems unwise. The group of mediums agrees to come with me.

As we pick our way between the tombstones, a sudden shriek makes my heart pound – until I realise it’s coming from a group of teenagers messing around.

The interruption brings home why some residents have become weary of Pluckley’s ghostly fame. Many villagers have relatives buried in this churchyard, and what feels like spooky entertainment to visitors can be intrusive to the people who live here.

Having said goodbye to Sue and the others, I walk back towards The Dering Arms on one final ghost hunt. I pass Rose Cottage, searching for the Tudor lady, and the garden of Greystones, where a black-robed monk is said to walk. Near the site of the former brickworks, I listen for the Screaming Man.

But I feel completely alone in the dark.

I foolishly take a selfie, and the bright flash leaves me temporarily night-blind. I quicken my pace, eyes still dazzled, when a dark shadow flits across the road in front of me.

Fear surges through me. I run.

The morning after

The next morning, daylight streams through my arched window at The Dering Arms and I feel rather silly. What I saw was almost certainly a small animal. I’m laughing at myself as I go downstairs for breakfast.

“Any luck last night?” James asks, smiling because he already knows the answer.

I mention that it must be a relief that The Dering Arms isn’t notoriously haunted. I expect him to laugh, but he looks thoughtful.

“There are always a couple of things you can’t explain,” he says. “When I lived in the coach house out the back, there was one floorboard that squeaked when no one was there.

“Another time, I took my wife a cup of tea one morning and she thanked me for tucking her in. I’d been in the kitchen, but she’d felt someone physically snuggle her in bed.”

His story surprises me more than any other. James had appeared to be an unequivocal non-believer – but even he admits that the village holds a few mysteries.

Pluckley was recorded in the Domesday Book, but people have lived on this small patch of land for far longer. For centuries, people have lived, loved, lost, hurt and been hurt here. If spirits really do remain, perhaps they aren’t the cinematic ghosts visitors hope to find – not a cowled monk or a ghostly Tudor lady, but the flickering traces of ordinary people.

Where to eat and stay in Pluckley

The Dering Arms: Set in a former hunting lodge beside Pluckley railway station, this characterful pub and restaurant has three double guest rooms. It makes a convenient base for exploring the village and surrounding countryside. Check current room availability and restaurant opening times before travelling.

The Black Horse: This historic country pub sits in the heart of the village and leans into Pluckley’s haunted reputation. Stop for lunch or dinner and ask the team about the strange events they claim to have witnessed. Check opening hours and food service times in advance, particularly if visiting during the week.

Getting there

Pluckley has a railway station on the line between London and Ashford. The station is beside The Dering Arms and around two miles from the centre of the village, so allow time to walk or arrange a taxi in advance. Sights are spread out along country lanes, making a car useful if you plan to explore several locations.

If driving, Pluckley is within easy reach of the M20 via junction 9 although parking in the village is limited.
